evidence_item.title: Genesis 2:4 as literary hinge
evidence_item.description: Genesis 2:4 uses the *toledot* formula at the transition from Genesis 1:1–2:3 into the garden narrative; the following scene narrows attention to land, the human, and the garden. The relationship between the units is interpreted in more than one way.
evidence_item.confidence_rationale: The formula and shift of focus are explicit; the literary relationship is a disputed scholarly inference.
evidence_item.passage_relevance: Genesis 2:4 uses the *toledot* formula at the transition from Genesis 1:1–2:3 into the garden narrative; the following scene narrows attention to land, the human, and the garden. The relationship between the units is interpreted in more than one way. This supports passage-specific synthesis of Genesis 2 while preserving the stated limits.
evidence_item.primary_observation: The chapter places “these are the generations/account of the heavens and the earth” at 2:4 and shifts from the ordered creation sequence to a focused garden-and-human scene.
evidence_item.scholarly_interpretation: Schmid treats the two units as distinct accounts joined in the received text; other readings emphasize complementary focus or harmonization. This evidence records the debate and does not settle contradiction or harmonization.

related_objects.notes: The passage is part of the book’s creation material.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The *toledot* formula and transition are stated at this verse.

evidence_item.title: The phrase *ezer kenegdo*
evidence_item.description: Genesis 2:18 and 2:20 describes the needed partner as *ezer kenegdo*, a helper corresponding to or facing the human. The phrase answers the “not good to be alone” problem and culminates in recognition of a matching human partner.
evidence_item.confidence_rationale: The Hebrew phrase and narrative correspondence are explicit; wider social conclusions are disputed.
evidence_item.passage_relevance: Genesis 2:18 and 2:20 describes the needed partner as *ezer kenegdo*, a helper corresponding to or facing the human. evidence_item.primary_observation: No animal is found as a corresponding helper; the woman is brought to the human and recognized as kin.
evidence_item.scholarly_interpretation: The word *ezer* alone does not settle social rank, and the phrase should not be used to assert either automatic subordination or a technical equality formula without further argument.

evidence_item.confidence_rationale: The sign’s function is explicit and its physical form unspecified; the racialized reception is documented historically.

evidence_item.title: Genesis 5 chronological figures across textual traditions
evidence_item.description: The begetting ages and lifespan figures in Genesis 5 differ among the Masoretic Text, Septuagint, and Samaritan Pentateuch. Comparative textual study treats these figures as a textual-critical question. This evidence records the variant traditions without selecting an original reading, recalculating dates, or altering the Scripture dataset.
evidence_item.confidence_rationale: The differences among the textual traditions are documented in comparative textual study; the original form and history of the readings remain disputed.
evidence_item.passage_relevance: The begetting ages and lifespan figures in Genesis 5 differ among the Masoretic Text, Septuagint, and Samaritan Pentateuch. Comparative textual study treats these figures as a textual-critical question.
